title: Guarded Admission Orchestrator and Proportional Shedder for Cross-Region Bursts
creator: Sofia Martinez
description: Implement a coordinated admission controller (Guarded Admission Orchestrator) paired with a proportional shedding algorithm to gracefully handle large tenant bursts across multiple regions and during limiter outages. Focus is on maintaining SLOs for latency and availability, preserving fairness across tenants, and providing clear observability and automated recovery paths.
background: Recent incidents (2025-01-29) exposed two failure modes: regional limiter process crashes causing uncoordinated spikes in downstream queues, and simultaneous multi-region bursts from a small set of tenants that starved others for capacity.

Existing mitigation patterns are ad-hoc: local soft-stops, emergency-wide static quotas, and manual tenant blacklisting during incidents. These lack proportionality and make SLO attainment inconsistent.
We need a coordinated, SLO-aware admission layer that survives partial limiter outages and rebalances requests proportionally when capacity is constrained.
goals: Maintain 99th percentile request latency SLOs across regions during moderate bursts (defined as up to 4x baseline per-tenant traffic) and limited limiter outages (single-region limiter down for up to 90s).
Enforce tenant fairness: no single tenant should consume more than its weighted share for >60s under sustained burst scenarios unless explicitly elevated by contract.

Enable seamless failover: when a limiter process in a region is unhealthy, orchestrator should reroute admissions to standby region variants or apply proportional shedding without full service interruption.
Ship robust telemetry and an automated runbook to reduce incident MTTR for limiter-related outages by 50%.
acceptance_criteria: Integration tests simulate multi-region bursts with 200 tenants and show at most 20% SLO violations compared to baseline for <120s events.
Chaos tests kill regional limiter process and system keeps accepting requests with degraded but predictable quality (latency within SLO after 30s warmup).
Dashboard: per-tenant admission rate, shed-rate, grace-token exhaustion, and regional limiter health are visible and emit alerts at defined thresholds.
A migration plan exists and has been validated in staging with two production-like regions and opt-in customer traffic.
design_notes: Architecture: lightweight central orchestrator agents run in each region. They exchange compact heartbeats and exchange per-epoch lease allocations using an optimistic lease token with lamport timestamps.

Admission flow: request arrives -> local agent evaluates local limiter status and local backlog -> consults local cache of global leases -> decide: admit, queue (short backpressure), or shed proportionally.

Proportional shedding: compute shed fraction = max(0, (observed_load - allocated_capacity) / observed_load) applied per-tenant with tenant weight multipliers (contractual weight + recent usage decay).
Grace tokens: short-lived credits issued to tenants during normal traffic to absorb tiny bursts without shedding; tokens decay and refill rate is workload-profile driven.

Outage handling: if agent detects local limiter unhealthy, agent enters guarded-failover mode: lower admission cap, increase grace token conservation, and broadcast 'limited' flag to other regions to inform routing policies.
Fallbacks: automatic fallback to compatible model variants (smaller context/quantized) is supported but toggled via rollout config to avoid quality cliffs.
Observability: add fine-grained histograms for admission latency, shed decision latency, and per-tenant fair_share_utilization.
State: keep orchestrator state soft (reconcilable) to survive partitioning; persist minimal checkpoints for quicker warm-starts.
tradeoffs: Centralized coordination vs. local speed: we chose lightweight peer-to-peer lease exchange to avoid global single point of failure; this adds eventual consistency windows where short unfairness can occur.
Grace tokens improve UX for small bursts but add complexity to accounting and potential temporary unfairness when tokens drain unevenly.
Proportional shedding reduces hard-cut customer impact vs strict blacklist, but introduces more complex telemetry to detect misconfigurations and tuning needs.
Fallback to lower-capacity model variants preserves availability at cost of output quality; must be carefully exposed to customers to avoid surprises.
telemetry_requirements: Per-region admission_rate (per-second) broken down by tenant tier and model route.
Per-tenant shed_rate and avg shed_fraction over sliding windows (1m/5m/1h).
Grace token balance per-tenant and refill/consumption rates.
Limiter health: last heartbeat, backlog queue depth, CPU/GPU saturation metrics, and lease skew across agents.
Synthetic SLO canaries: repeated small synthetic requests to measure end-to-end latency and error rates during rollouts.
Alerting: fire high-severity when aggregate shed_rate > 15% and SLO breach > 1% for 5m.
test_plan: Unit tests for admission decision math (edge cases: zero allocated capacity, tenants with zero weight, token underflow).
Integration tests across 3-region cluster simulating 400% burst from 5 tenants and random limiter kills.
Chaos: randomized network partitions and process restarts with assertions on eventual SLO recovery and no deadlocks.
Performance bench: ensure admission decision latency < 1.5ms p95 in hot path when batching is enabled.
Load tests with billing simulation to confirm weighted share enforcement under traffic mix (short/long requests).
rollout_plan: Feature gate behind config flag per-cluster. Stage 1: enable orchestrator in observe-only mode (no shedding) in staging and one low-traffic prod region.
Stage 2: enable guarded-failover and proportional shedding for 2% of traffic (canary customers) with fast rollback.
Stage 3: expand to 25% traffic after 72h with monitoring runbook checks and on-call signoffs.
Stage 4: global enablement with customer opt-in toggles for fallback model variant usage.
Rollback: automated rollback if synthetic SLO canaries exceed thresholds or shed_rate unexpectedly rises >30% within 10m.
migration_plan: Backward-compatible: agents can be safely deployed side-by-side with legacy limiter. Start with observe-only mode to gather metrics and tune weights.
Customer opt-in: allow customers to pin to legacy flow until 2025-06-01; provide tooling to simulate shedding behavior for customers.
Data migration: no heavy state migration required; graceful mode reads legacy quotas and maps to initial lease allocations.
Runtime toggles: per-tenant knobs for grace_token parameters and weight overrides (support via Console UI and API).
notes_and_progress_updates: 2025-02-16: Kickoff meeting with SRE and PM. Agreed on SLO targets and the three-stage rollout plan. Action: SRE to sketch heartbeat protocol.
2025-02-20: Prototype of lease exchange implemented (optimistic token + epoch). Observed 120ms median convergence across regions; optimizing to target <50ms.
2025-02-28: Design review with Marco and Janelle. Design feedback: simplify grace-token UI and add per-tenant override audit trail. Janelle to provide wireframes.
2025-03-03: Integration tests added for chaos cases. Early results show proportional shedding reduces max tenant unfairness by ~60% in synthetic tests.
2025-03-05: Security reviewed initial design; no high risks but recommend limiting fallback-model list to approved artifacts. Action: add release gating for fallback-models.
open_questions: What should the maximum grace-token refill rate be for free-tier tenants vs enterprise?
How long do we allow cross-region warmup before we consider a region unhealthy and start failover? 30s or 90s?
Is per-request routing to another region acceptable for legal/data residency sensitive tenants, or do we need per-tenant routing constraints enforced?
